blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site against the official GATE 2027 CS syllabus from IIT Madras. The questions are original and in the style of GATE: they drill the concepts GATE repeats, they are not copies of past papers. If the official syllabus changes, the official PDF wins.

GATE gives short C programs and asks for the output, so the skill is tracing exactly what the language guarantees. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a 32-bit `int` (4 bytes), `char` is 1 byte, pointers are 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine, and `double` is 8 bytes.

### Operators, precedence and conversions

| Precedence (high to low) | Operators | Associativity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | postfix `++ --`, `()`, `[]`, `.`, `->` | left to right |
| 2 | prefix `++ --`, unary `+ - ! ~ * &`, `sizeof`, casts | right to left |
| 3 | `* / %` | left to right |
| 4 | `+ -` | left to right |
| 5 | `<< >>` | left to right |
| 6 | `< <= > >=` | left to right |
| 7 | `== !=` | left to right |
| 8, 9, 10 | `&`, then `^`, then `\|` | left to right |
| 11, 12 | `&&`, then `\|\|` | left to right |
| 13 | `?:` | right to left |
| 14 | `= += -= …` | right to left |

- **Integer division truncates toward zero** and `%` takes the sign of the dividend (C99): `7 / 2 = 3`, `-7 / 2 = -3`, `-7 % 3 = -1`.
- **`7 / 2 * 2`** is `(7 / 2) * 2 = 6`, not 7: division happens first, in integers.
- **Mixing signed and unsigned** converts the signed value to unsigned. `-1 < 1u` is **false (0)**, because -1 becomes a huge unsigned number.
- **`&&` and `||` short-circuit.** In `a++ && b++` with `a = 0`, `b++` never runs, but `a++` still increments `a`.
- **Bitwise precedence trap:** `5 & 3 | 4 ^ 1` is `(5 & 3) | (4 ^ 1) = 1 | 5 = 5`.
- **Macros are textual.** With `#define SQR(x) x*x`, `SQR(2+1)` expands to `2+1*2+1 = 5`, not 9. Always parenthesise.
- **`x++` yields the old value, `++x` the new one.** `int j = i++ * 2;` with `i = 5` gives `j = 10` and `i = 6`.
- **`static` locals keep their value between calls** and are initialised once.

blocks.title: Static variable

blocks.text: Expressions such as `i = i++ + ++i` or `a[i] = i++` modify and read a variable without a sequence point. If a question is only valid when you assume an order, the intended answer is usually "undefined" or the question avoids it. Don't invent an order.
blocks.title: Undefined behaviour is not an exam answer

blocks.text:
- **Evaluate step by step on paper,** keeping a column for each variable. Update the variable column after each statement.
- **Integer first, float last:** `7 / 2 * 2.0` is `3 * 2.0 = 6.0`, but `7 / 2.0 * 2` is 7.0.
- **Look for a trap:** short-circuit, a macro without brackets, an unsigned comparison, a `static` local, a missing `break` in a `switch`, or `=` where `==` was meant.
- **`printf("%d", x)` of a `char` or `short`** promotes it to `int`; `%d` with a `double` is wrong.
- **`switch` falls through** to the next case unless there is a `break`.
blocks.title: C output cheat codes

blocks.text:
### Pointers and arrays

- An array name decays to a pointer to its first element, and `a[i]` is `*(a + i)`. **Pointer arithmetic scales by the element size**: `p + 1` moves 4 bytes for an `int *`.
- `*p++` increments the pointer after reading, but `(*p)++` increments the pointed-to value. `*++p` increments first.
- `p[-1]` is `*(p - 1)`. With `int a[] = {10,20,30,40}; int *p = a + 1; p++;` then `*p` is 30 and `p[-1]` is 20.
- `sizeof(a)` for an array is the total bytes, but for a pointer parameter it is just the pointer size.
- A **pointer to pointer** `**q` dereferences twice: with `int x = 5, *p = &x, **q = &p;`, writing `**q = 9` sets `x = 9`.

### Two-dimensional arrays

C stores `int a[R][C]` in **row-major** order. The address of `a[i][j]` is `base + (i·C + j) · size`. For `int a[3][4]` at 1000, `a[2][1]` is at 1000 + (2·4 + 1)·4 = 1036.

### Strings

A C string is a `char` array ending in `'\0'`. `char s[] = "GATE";` has `sizeof(s) = 5` (four letters and the terminator) and `strlen(s) = 4`. `strlen` counts up to, not including, the terminator.

### Structures, padding and unions

Each member sits at an address that is a multiple of its own size (alignment), and the struct's total size is padded to a multiple of its largest member's alignment.

blocks.code:
struct A { char a; int b; char c; };  // a at 0, 3 bytes padding, b at 4, c at 8, 3 padding: size 12
struct B { int b; char a; char c; };  // b at 0, a at 4, c at 5, 2 padding: size 8
union  U { int i; double d; char c; };// all members share the same bytes: size = largest = 8
blocks.title: Padding

blocks.text:
Reordering members from large to small usually shrinks a struct. A union's size is the size of its largest member.

### Memory and parameter passing

- **C passes parameters by value.** A function that changes its own copy does not change the caller's variable. To modify the caller's variable pass its address.
- `malloc` memory that is never `free`d is a **memory leak**. Using memory after `free`, or returning the address of a local variable, gives a **dangling pointer** and undefined behaviour.

blocks.code:
void f(int a, int *b) { a = a + 1; *b = *b + 1; }
// int x = 1, y = 1; f(x, &y);   x stays 1, y becomes 2
blocks.title: Call by value and by address

blocks.text:
- **Draw boxes and arrows.** Write each variable's value and address and follow every `*` and `&`.
- **`p + n` moves n elements, not n bytes.** The difference of two pointers is also in elements.
- **Struct size:** list member offsets, align each to its size, then pad the total to the largest alignment.
- **`sizeof("GATE")` is 5**, `strlen("GATE")` is 4.
- **Row-major address** = base + (i × columns + j) × element size.
- **Returning a pointer to a local array is a bug.** The array dies when the function returns.
blocks.title: Pointer cheat codes

blocks.text:
### The call stack

Each call pushes an **activation record** (parameters, return address, locals). When the function returns the record is popped. A recursion that goes n levels deep before returning has **n + 1 records** on the stack at its deepest, and a recursion with no base case overflows the stack.

### Recursion patterns to recognise

| Function | Result or count |
|---|---|
| `f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2)`, `f(0)=f(1)=1` | f(6) = 13; the number of calls to compute f(n) is 2f(n) − 1 |
| `power(x, y) = x * power(x, y-1)` | y + 1 calls, time linear in y |
| `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)` | stops when b = 0; at most O(log min) calls |
| Tower of Hanoi `H(n) = 2H(n-1) + 1` | 2ⁿ − 1 moves |
| Binary recursion `g(n-1), print n, g(n-1)` | prints the "ruler sequence": g(3) prints 1 2 1 3 1 2 1 |

blocks.title: Ruler sequence

blocks.text:
A call is **tail recursive** if the recursive call is the very last thing done, with no pending work: `return fact(n-1, n*acc);` is tail recursive, but `return n * fact(n-1);` is not. A compiler can turn tail recursion into a loop and use constant stack space.

### Scoping rules

- **Static (lexical) scoping,** which C uses: a free variable refers to the declaration visible where the function is **written**.
- **Dynamic scoping:** it refers to the most recent declaration on the **call stack**.

blocks.title: Static versus dynamic scope

blocks.text:
- **Draw the recursion tree.** The number of calls is the number of nodes, and the stack depth is the height of the tree plus one.
- **Fibonacci-style calls:** calls(n) = 1 + calls(n-1) + calls(n-2). With calls(0) = calls(1) = 1: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25. The 15 is the number of calls for n = 5.
- **Print before or after the recursive call?** Printing before gives pre-order, after gives post-order.
- **Dynamic scoping = look at who called me.** Static scoping = look at where I was written.
- **Hanoi moves:** 2ⁿ − 1. For 5 disks that is 31.
blocks.title: Recursion cheat codes

blocks.text:
### Array address formulas

For a one-dimensional array `A[lb..ub]`: address of `A[i]` = base + (i − lb) × w. For a two-dimensional `A[l1..u1][l2..u2]` with n₂ = u2 − l2 + 1 columns:

- **Row-major:** base + ((i − l1) × n₂ + (j − l2)) × w
- **Column-major:** base + ((j − l2) × n₁ + (i − l1)) × w, where n₁ is the number of rows

For `A[1..5][1..8]`, row-major, base 2000, w = 4: `A[3][4]` is at 2000 + (2·8 + 3)·4 = 2076.

A lower-triangular n × n matrix needs only n(n + 1)/2 cells. Stored row by row with 1-based indices, `a[i][j]` (i ≥ j) is at position i(i − 1)/2 + j. So `a[5][3]` is at 13.

### Stacks

A stack is last-in first-out with **push**, **pop** and **peek** in O(1).

- **Postfix evaluation:** scan left to right, push operands, and on an operator pop two, apply, push the result. `5 3 + 2 * 7 -` gives (5 + 3) × 2 − 7 = 9.
- **Infix to postfix:** operands go straight to the output, operators wait on a stack until a lower-or-equal precedence operator arrives. `A + B * C - D` becomes `A B C * + D -`.
- **Balanced brackets, next-greater-element and undo** all use a stack.
- **Stack permutations:** if 1, 2, …, n are pushed in order, with pops allowed at any time, the number of possible pop sequences is the Catalan number Cₙ (14 for n = 4). A sequence is impossible if it needs a larger number to come out before a smaller one that was pushed earlier but is not on top. With 1, 2, 3 pushed in order, **3, 1, 2** cannot happen.

### Queues

A queue is first-in first-out with **enqueue** and **dequeue** in O(1) using a linked list or a circular array. In a circular array of size N with `front` and `rear` indices, the elements are (rear − front + N) mod N + 1 when the queue is non-empty and `rear` points at the last element. A **deque** allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

A queue can be built from **two stacks** (push onto one, pour into the other for dequeue). Each element moves at most twice, so n enqueues and n dequeues take O(n) in total, i.e. O(1) amortised per operation.

- **Postfix by hand:** scan, push numbers, and the top two items are the operands (the second item popped is the left operand).
- **Stack permutations:** number of valid pop orders = Catalan(n). Test a candidate by simulating push and pop.
- **Circular queue count:** (rear − front + N) mod N + 1 when `rear` is the last element's index.
- **Operator order in infix → postfix:** equal precedence pops first for left-associative operators.
- **Triangular matrix:** n(n+1)/2 cells and row-by-row position i(i−1)/2 + j.
blocks.title: Stack and queue cheat codes

blocks.text:
| Operation | Singly (head only) | Doubly |
|---|---|---|
| Insert at head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Insert at tail | **O(n)** (O(1) with a tail pointer) | O(n) / O(1) with tail |
| Delete the head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Delete a node **given a pointer to it** | O(n) to find the previous node (O(1) trick: copy the next node over it, if it is not the last) | **O(1)** |
| Search | O(n) | O(n) |
| Reverse | O(n) time, O(1) extra space | O(n) |

**Two-pointer techniques:** a slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two. When the fast pointer reaches the end of a list of 9 nodes, the slow pointer is at node 5, the middle. If the list has a cycle the two pointers eventually meet (**Floyd's tortoise and hare**), which detects a cycle in O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.title: Walk to the second-last node

blocks.text:
- **Draw the nodes and the pointer after each statement.** Most output questions are lost by skipping one step.
- **Reversal needs three pointers** (previous, current, next) and runs in one pass.
- **O(1) deletion needs a doubly linked list** or a pointer to the *previous* node.
- **A tail pointer makes enqueue O(1)** for a singly linked queue.
- **Middle and cycle problems = slow and fast pointers.**
blocks.title: Linked-list cheat codes

blocks.text:
### Binary tree facts

For a binary tree with root at height 0:

- Maximum nodes at level i is 2ⁱ, and in a tree of height h is **2^(h+1) − 1**. Minimum height of n nodes is ⌊log₂ n⌋.
- If every internal node has exactly two children, **leaves = internal nodes + 1**. A full tree with 20 leaves has 19 internal nodes and 39 nodes in all.
- The number of different **shapes** of binary trees with n nodes is the Catalan number Cₙ: C₄ = 14. With distinct labelled nodes it is Cₙ × n!.
- A **complete** tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋ (100 nodes → 6).

### Traversals

| Order | Visit | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Preorder | root, left, right | copy a tree |
| Inorder | left, root, right | sorted order of a BST |
| Postorder | left, right, root | delete a tree, evaluate expressions |
| Level order | by depth | BFS with a queue |

**Rebuilding a tree:** the inorder sequence together with either the preorder or the postorder sequence determines the tree. Preorder and postorder alone do **not** (unless every internal node has two children). Method: the first preorder item (or last postorder item) is the root; find it in the inorder sequence to split into left and right subtrees; repeat.

Example: preorder A B D E C F and inorder D B E A F C give the postorder **D E B F C A**.

### Binary search trees

Left subtree < node < right subtree. Search, insert and delete cost **O(h)**: O(log n) when balanced and **O(n)** for a skewed tree, which is what sorted insertion order gives. The inorder traversal of a BST is sorted. To delete a node with two children, replace it by its **inorder successor** (the smallest key in the right subtree) or predecessor, then delete that node. The number of insertion orders that give the same BST is a count of ways to interleave the left and right insertions: for keys 1, 2, 3 the tree with root 2 arises from the orders 2,1,3 and 2,3,1.

### AVL trees

An AVL tree keeps |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1 at every node, restoring it by rotations (LL, RR, LR, RL). The minimum number of nodes N(h) of an AVL tree of height h satisfies **N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1** with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2, so N = 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20 … The height is O(log n), at most about 1.44 log₂ n.

- **Rebuild from traversals:** inorder splits, preorder (or postorder from the back) names the root. Always start from the root.
- **Full binary tree:** L = I + 1, so n = 2L − 1.
- **Skewed BST** comes from inserting sorted keys, so its height is n − 1.
- **BST traversal from a preorder list:** the first element is the root; elements smaller than it come first (left subtree), then the larger ones.
- **AVL minimum nodes:** 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20. Each is the previous two plus 1.
- **Preorder + postorder gives a unique tree only for full trees.**
blocks.title: Tree cheat codes

blocks.text:
A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree stored in an array with the heap property: in a **max-heap** every parent is ≥ its children (a min-heap is the reverse). Using 1-based indexing, the parent of `i` is `⌊i/2⌋`, and the children of `i` are `2i` and `2i + 1`. The parent of `a[11]` is `a[5]`.

| Operation | Method | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Insert | add at the end, sift up | O(log n) |
| Extract max/min | move the last element to the root, sift down | O(log n) |
| Peek | read `a[1]` | O(1) |
| **Build heap** from n elements | sift down from ⌊n/2⌋ to 1 | **O(n)** |
| Heapsort | build heap, then n extractions | O(n log n) |
| Search for an arbitrary key | no structure helps | O(n) |

- The leaves are the nodes with index > ⌊n/2⌋, so there are ⌈n/2⌉ leaves (5 for n = 10).
- The height is ⌊log₂ n⌋.
- Inserting 10, 20, 15, 30, 25 one by one into a max-heap gives the array **30 25 15 10 20**.
- The number of different max-heaps on n distinct keys: 1, 1, 2, 3, 8, 20 for n = 1 … 6. For {1,2,3,4} there are 3.

- **Draw the tree while you sift.** Compare with the parent only on the way up, with the larger child on the way down.
- **Build-heap is linear** because most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little.
- **The k-th smallest of a min-heap is not at a fixed place,** so finding it needs k extractions: O(k log n).
- **Largest element of a min-heap** is at one of the leaves, so locating it costs O(n).
- **Parent = ⌊i/2⌋, children = 2i, 2i+1** (for a 0-based array: (i − 1)/2, 2i + 1, 2i + 2).
blocks.title: Heap cheat codes

blocks.text:
A graph G = (V, E). Two standard representations:

| | Adjacency matrix | Adjacency list |
|---|---|---|
| Space | O(V²) | O(V + E) |
| Is (u, v) an edge? | O(1) | O(degree) |
| List all neighbours | O(V) | O(degree) |
| Best for | dense graphs | sparse graphs |

- **BFS** uses a queue and visits vertices in order of distance from the source. **DFS** uses a stack or recursion. Both take **O(V + E)** with adjacency lists.
- With edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E and neighbours visited alphabetically from A: BFS order A B C D E, DFS order **A B D C E**.
- The number of **connected components** equals the number of times you must start a fresh DFS or BFS.
- A **topological order** exists only for a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The edges a→c, b→c, c→d have exactly two topological orders (a b c d and b a c d).
- For an adjacency matrix A of a simple undirected graph, (Aᵏ)[i][j] counts walks of length k from i to j, and **trace(A³) / 6 is the number of triangles**.

- **Pick the representation by density:** E close to V² → matrix, E close to V → list.
- **Trace DFS with the recursion stack.** Remember to go back up after a dead end.
- **Counting components:** count the DFS restarts.
- **Counting topological orders:** repeatedly pick any vertex with in-degree 0 and multiply the choices.
- **Detect a cycle** in an undirected graph by seeing an already-visited vertex that is not the parent.
blocks.title: Graph cheat codes

sections.title: Cheat sheet: Programming and Data Structures on one page

blocks.text:
| Topic | Fact |
|---|---|
| Integer division | truncates toward zero; `%` follows the dividend's sign |
| Short-circuit | `&&`, `\|\|` skip the right side |
| Macro pitfall | `SQR(x) x*x` with `SQR(2+1)` is 5 |
| Pointer arithmetic | `p + 1` moves one element |
| Row-major address | base + (i·C + j)·size |
| Struct size | align members, pad to the largest alignment |
| Fibonacci calls | 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25 |
| Hanoi | 2ⁿ − 1 moves |
| Stack pop sequences | Catalan(n) |
| Postfix evaluation | push operands; operator pops two |
| BST | O(h); inorder is sorted |
| Rebuild a tree | inorder + preorder or postorder |
| Full binary tree | leaves = internal + 1 |
| AVL minimum nodes | N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 |
| Heap | parent ⌊i/2⌋, children 2i and 2i+1; build O(n) |
| BFS and DFS | O(V + E) with lists |
| Triangles | trace(A³) / 6 |

60 original GATE-style questions on 8 areas. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people. The marks shown are what a question like this would carry in GATE; in the real exam a wrong 1-mark MCQ costs 1/3 mark and a wrong 2-mark MCQ costs 2/3.

items.q:
*(1 mark)* What is the output of the following C statement?
```c
printf("%d", 7 / 2 * 2);
```
items.w: Division and multiplication group left to right, and 7 / 2 is integer division: (7 / 2) * 2 = 3 * 2 = 6. (7 would need the multiplication first.)

items.q:
*(1 mark)* Assuming C99 semantics (division truncates toward zero), the output of the following statement is
```c
printf("%d", -7 % 3);
```
items.w: In C99 a / b truncates toward zero, and a % b has the sign of the dividend: -7 / 3 = -2 and -7 % 3 = -7 - 3(-2) = -1.
i++ yields the old value 5, so j = 5 * 2 = 10. Afterwards i has been incremented to 6, so the output is "6 10".

items.q:
*(2 marks)* The value of x after the following declaration is
```c
int x = 2 + 3 * 4 % 5 - 1;
```
items.w: *, / and % share a precedence level and associate left to right: (3 * 4) % 5 = 12 % 5 = 2. Then x = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3.

items.q:
*(2 marks)* The output of the following C statement is
```c
printf("%d", 5 & 3 | 4 ^ 1);
```
items.w: Bitwise precedence is & then ^ then |. So (5 & 3) | (4 ^ 1) = 1 | 5 = 5.

items.q:
*(2 marks)* Given the macro below, what is the value of SQR(2+1)?
```c
#define SQR(x) x*x
```
items.w: The macro substitutes text: 2+1*2+1. Multiplication is evaluated first, so the value is 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
a++ evaluates to the old value 0 (false) and a becomes 1. Because the left operand of && is false, the right operand b++ is never evaluated, so b stays 0. Output "1 0".

items.q:
*(2 marks)* Assuming a 32-bit int, the output of the following statement is
```c
printf("%d", -1 < 1u);
```
items.w: The int -1 is converted to unsigned, giving 4294967295, which is not less than 1. The comparison is false, so 0 is printed.
The static variable c is initialised once and keeps its value between calls. The calls return 1, 2 and 3, and the last value is printed.
p starts at a[1] and after p++ points to a[2] = 30. p[-1] is a[1] = 20. Output "30 20".
The array holds the four letters and the terminating '\0', so sizeof(s) = 5. strlen counts the characters before '\0': 4.

items.q:
*(2 marks)* Assuming int is 4 bytes and must be aligned to a multiple of 4, the size of the following structure is
```c
struct S { char a; int b; char c; };
```
items.w: a is at offset 0, then 3 bytes of padding, b at offsets 4 to 7, c at offset 8, and 3 bytes of trailing padding so that the size is a multiple of 4: 12 bytes. (Declaring b first would give 8.)

items.q:
*(2 marks)* On a machine where int is 4 bytes, double is 8 bytes and char is 1 byte, the size of the following union is
```c
union U { int i; double d; char c; };
```
items.w: All members of a union share the same storage, so its size is that of the largest member, a double: 8 bytes.

items.q: *(2 marks)* An array int a[3][4] is stored in row-major order starting at address 1000, and int is 4 bytes. The address of a[2][1] is

items.w: q points to p and p points to x, so **q is x itself. Assigning 9 through it changes x.
x is passed by value, so the function increments only its copy. y is passed by address, so the function modifies the caller's y. Output "1 2".

items.q: *(1 mark)* A function returns the address of one of its local (automatic) variables. Using that pointer in the caller
o: frees the memory of the variable
gives a dangling pointer and undefined behaviour
items.w: The local variable lives in the function's activation record, which is gone after the return. Dereferencing the pointer is undefined behaviour.

items.q:
*(2 marks)* What is the value of f(6) for the function below?
```c
int f(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return f(n - 1) + f(n - 2); }
```
*(2 marks)* For the same function f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) with f(0) = f(1) = 1, the total number of calls to f (including the first call) made to evaluate f(5) is
items.w: Let calls(n) = 1 + calls(n−1) + calls(n−2) with calls(0) = calls(1) = 1: 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 15. So 15 calls.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The function gcd(a, b) is defined as: if b == 0 return a, else return gcd(b, a % b). The total number of calls to gcd (including the first) made by gcd(48, 18) is
items.w: gcd(48,18) → gcd(18,12) → gcd(12,6) → gcd(6,0). That is 4 calls, and the result is 6.

Under dynamic scoping a free variable is resolved through the chain of callers. f is called from g, where x = 20 is the most recent binding, so 20 is printed. (Under static scoping, as in C itself, the global x = 10 would be used.)

items.q: *(1 mark)* Which of the following functions is tail recursive?
o: int f(int n, int acc) { if (n == 0) return acc; return f(n - 1, n * acc); }
int f(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return f(n - 1) + f(n - 2); }
int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return n * f(n - 1); }
int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return f(n - 1) + 1; }
items.w: In (a) the recursive call is the last action and its value is returned unchanged. In (b), (c) and (d) the result of the call is multiplied or added to something after it returns.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A function f(n) calls f(n − 1) (and does nothing else recursive) with f(0) as the base case. The maximum number of activation records on the call stack while evaluating f(10) is
items.w: The calls are f(10), f(9), …, f(0): 11 activation records are on the stack when the deepest call is running.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The minimum number of moves needed to solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle with 5 disks is
items.w: H(n) = 2H(n−1) + 1 with H(0) = 0, which gives 2ⁿ − 1 = 31 for n = 5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The value of the postfix expression 5 3 + 2 * 7 - is
*(2 marks)* The postfix form of the infix expression A + B * C - D is
items.w: B * C binds tighter than +, giving A (BC*) + then − D: ABC*+D-.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The numbers 1, 2, 3 are pushed onto a stack in this order, and pops may be interleaved with the pushes. Which of the following output sequences is NOT possible?
items.w: To pop 3 first, both 1 and 2 must already be on the stack beneath it. Then 2 is above 1, so 2 comes out before 1. The sequence 3, 1, 2 is impossible.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed in this order onto a stack, with pops interleaved arbitrarily. The number of different possible output sequences is
items.w: The number of stack-permutations of n items is the Catalan number Cₙ = C(2n, n)/(n + 1). For n = 4 this is 70/5 = 14.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A circular queue is implemented in an array of size 8 with indices 0 to 7. front = 6 is the index of the first element and rear = 1 is the index of the last element. The number of elements in the queue is
items.w: The elements occupy indices 6, 7, 0, 1, which is (rear − front + 8) mod 8 + 1 = (1 − 6 + 8) mod 8 + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A queue is implemented with two stacks (enqueue pushes onto stack 1; dequeue pops from stack 2, refilling it from stack 1 when it is empty). The total worst-case time for n enqueue operations followed by n dequeue operations is
items.w: Each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total, once on each stack. So 2n operations cost O(n) in all, i.e. O(1) amortised each.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A two-dimensional array A[1..5][1..8] is stored in row-major order starting at address 2000, and each element takes 4 bytes. The address of A[3][4] is
*(2 marks)* The lower-triangular part (including the diagonal) of an n × n matrix is stored row by row in a one-dimensional array with 1-based positions. The position of element a[5][3] is
items.w: Rows 1 to 4 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 elements. Within row 5, the third element is next, so the position is 10 + 3 = 13 (formula i(i−1)/2 + j).

items.q: *(2 marks)* Given a pointer to a node in a doubly linked list (not the last node), the time to delete that node is
items.w: The node has links to both neighbours, so we update prev->next and next->prev directly without traversing the list.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A singly linked list has 9 nodes. A slow pointer moves one node per step and a fast pointer moves two nodes per step, both from the first node. When the fast pointer reaches the last node, the slow pointer is at node number
items.w: The fast pointer reaches node 9 after 4 steps (1 → 3 → 5 → 7 → 9). The slow pointer has moved 4 nodes, so it is at node 5, the middle.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The time and extra space needed to reverse a singly linked list of n nodes in place are
o: O(log n) time and O(1) space
items.w: One pass with three pointers (previous, current, next) reverses every link, so O(n) time, and no additional storage proportional to n.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In a singly linked list with only a head pointer, inserting a new node at the end takes
items.w: We must walk to the last node to reach it, taking O(n). With an extra tail pointer, the insertion would be O(1).

items.q: *(2 marks)* Which technique detects a cycle in a singly linked list using only O(1) extra space?
o: storing visited nodes in a hash table
a DFS with a visited array
items.w: Floyd's method moves one pointer by 1 and another by 2; if there is a cycle they meet. It needs only two pointers. The other methods use O(n) extra space.
The loop moves p until p->next->next is NULL. At node 3, p->next->next is node 5 (not NULL), so p moves to node 4. Now p->next is 5 and p->next->next is NULL, so it stops and prints 4.

items.q: *(1 mark)* The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 4 (the root is at height 0) is
items.w: A binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, which is 31 for h = 4.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A binary tree in which every internal node has exactly two children has 20 leaves. The total number of nodes is
items.w: In such a tree the number of leaves is one more than the number of internal nodes, so there are 19 internal nodes and 19 + 20 = 39 nodes in total.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of structurally different binary trees with 4 nodes is
items.w: The number of binary tree shapes with n nodes is the Catalan number Cₙ. C₄ = C(8, 4) / 5 = 14.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A binary tree has preorder A B D E C F and inorder D B E A F C. Its postorder traversal is
o: D B E F C A
D E B C F A
D E B F C A
E D B F C A
items.w: A is the root. The inorder sequence splits into left (D B E) and right (F C). In the left part B is the root with D and E as children. In the right part C is the root with F as its left child. Postorder: D E B F C A.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Keys 10, 5, 15, 3, 7, 12, 20, 1 are inserted in this order into an empty binary search tree. The height of the tree (the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path) is
items.w: 10 is the root; 5 and 15 are its children; 3 and 7 are children of 5; 12 and 20 are children of 15; 1 is the left child of 3. The longest path 10 → 5 → 3 → 1 has 3 edges.

items.q: *(2 marks)* How many different insertion orders of the keys 1, 2, 3 into an empty BST produce the same tree as the order 2, 1, 3?
items.w: The root must be 2. After that, 1 and 3 can be inserted in either order: 2, 1, 3 and 2, 3, 1. Both give the same shape.

items.q: *(2 marks)* An AVL tree has height 4, where the height of a single node is 0. The minimum number of nodes it can have is
*(2 marks)* In a BST with root 50, left child 30, right child 70, and 70 has left child 60 and right child 80, the root 50 is deleted by replacing it with its inorder successor. The new root is
items.w: The inorder successor of 50 is the smallest key in its right subtree, which is 60 (the left child of 70). Node 60 replaces 50 and is removed from its old place.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The preorder traversal of a binary search tree is 8, 3, 1, 6, 4, 7, 10, 14, 13. Its postorder traversal is
items.w: Build the BST from the preorder sequence. Left of 8 is 3 (children 1 and 6, with 6 having children 4 and 7). Right of 8 is 10 with right child 14 whose left child is 13. Postorder visits children before parents.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A complete binary tree has 100 nodes. Its height (number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path) is
items.w: A complete tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋ = ⌊6.64⌋ = 6.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In a binary heap stored in an array a[1..n] with the root at a[1], the parent of a[11] is
items.w: The parent of index i is ⌊i/2⌋ = ⌊11/2⌋ = 5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The time needed to build a binary heap from n unsorted elements using the bottom-up (sift-down) method is
items.w: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down very few levels, so the total work is Σ (n / 2^(h+1)) · h = O(n), better than n separate insertions at O(n log n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The keys 10, 20, 15, 30, 25 are inserted one at a time, in this order, into an initially empty max-heap using sift-up. The resulting array (from index 1 to 5) is
*(2 marks)* A binary heap has 10 nodes. The number of leaf nodes is
items.w: The leaves occupy indices ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n, i.e. 6 to 10: ⌈10/2⌉ = 5 leaves.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of different arrays that are valid max-heaps when the keys 1, 2, 3, 4 are arranged as a binary heap is
items.w: The maximum 4 is the root. The element at index 2 must be larger than the element at index 4, its only child. Of the 6 arrangements of {1, 2, 3} in positions 2, 3, 4, exactly half satisfy that, so 3.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Breadth-first search on a graph stored as adjacency lists takes time
items.w: Each vertex is enqueued once and each adjacency list is scanned once, giving O(V + E).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A graph has edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D and D–E. Starting at A and always visiting neighbours in alphabetical order, the depth-first visiting order is
items.w: From A go to B, from B to D (B's only unvisited neighbour). D's neighbours are B (visited), C, E; visit C first. C has no new neighbours, so return to D and visit E. Order A B D C E.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A directed acyclic graph has edges a → c, b → c and c → d. The number of different topological orderings is
items.w: a and b must both precede c, which precedes d. The two orders of a and b give a b c d and b a c d.

items.q: *(2 marks)* An undirected graph has 8 vertices (1 to 8) and the edges 1–2, 2–3, 4–5, 6–7, 7–8 and 8–6. The number of connected components is
items.w: The components are {1, 2, 3}, {4, 5} and {6, 7, 8}. Each fresh DFS start finds one: 3 components.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph. The quantity trace(A³) / 6 equals
o: the number of vertices of degree 3
the number of paths of length 3
items.w: The diagonal entry (A³)[i][i] counts closed walks of length 3 through i, which are triangles through i counted twice (two directions). Summing over i counts each triangle 3 × 2 = 6 times.

blocks.text: #### Cheat sheet: Programming and Data Structures on one page

items.question: Why does `SQR(2+1)` give 5 and not 9 when `SQR(x)` is defined as `x*x`?
items.answer: The preprocessor substitutes text: `2+1*2+1`. Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so the value is 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. The macro should be `((x)*(x))`.

items.question: Reconstruct the tree whose preorder is A B D E C F and inorder is D B E A F C. What is its postorder?
items.answer: A is the root. In the inorder sequence D B E is the left subtree and F C the right. In the left part B is the root with D and E as children. In the right part C is the root with F as its left child. The postorder is D E B F C A.

items.question: Why can a heap be built in O(n) even though each sift-down costs O(log n)?
items.answer: Half of the nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter sift down at most one level, an eighth at most two, and so on. The sum n/4·1 + n/8·2 + … is linear.

items.question: What is the difference between static and dynamic scoping, and which does C use?
items.answer: Under static scoping a free variable is resolved in the environment where the function is defined; under dynamic scoping it is resolved through the chain of callers. C uses static scoping.
